entries.title: Earth’s moving plates
entries.answer: Earth’s stiff outer shell is broken into huge pieces called tectonic plates. They fit together a little like puzzle pieces, but they move very slowly. In some places, two plates pull apart and new ocean floor forms between them. In other places, one plate moves under another. Elsewhere, plates slide past each other. These motions help build mountains, make some volcanoes, and cause many earthquakes. The plates move over hot rock that is mostly solid. It can slowly change shape under pressure.
facts: A tectonic plate can hold both a continent and ocean floor.
Some plates move only a few inches in a year.

entries.title: How can a hill decide which river gets the rain?
entries.answer: A watershed is an area where water drains toward the same river, lake, or other low place. Rain falling on opposite sides of a ridge may reach different streams. A stream’s small watershed can fit inside a bigger one if the stream flows into a river. Water can take different routes along the surface or partly underground. Drawing the high ground around a river helps to map the land that sends water toward it.
facts: A watershed boundary often follows high ground.

entries.title: How can a river carve a deep canyon?
entries.answer: Water carrying sand and stones can wear away the bottom of a riverbed. Over a very long time a river may cut much deeper into the land. Rain, falling rocks, and side streams can wear away its sides. In a deep canyon, different layers of rock may show on the walls. Some form cliffs because they are harder to wear away. Other layers form slopes as pieces of rock break down.
facts: The Colorado River runs through the Grand Canyon.

entries.title: How can a rock float?
entries.answer: Pumice forms when particular kinds of melted rock have gas bubbles in them as they cool. After the rock hardens, it is full of holes where bubbles used to be. A piece of pumice can look solid from far away, but much of its inside may be empty space. That makes some pieces less dense than water, so they float. Water may later soak into the holes and change whether a piece floats.
facts: Pumice is volcanic rock.

entries.title: How can a solid rock change without melting?
entries.answer: A rock buried deep underground can warm up and be squeezed hard. Minerals may change shape or grow again, and new minerals may appear. The rock can change its pattern and strength while staying mostly solid. A rock changed this way is called metamorphic. Slate can come from a kind of muddy rock, and marble can come from limestone. A piece can keep clues about the rock it once was.
facts: Some metamorphic rocks split along flat layers.

entries.title: How can a whole river of ice move?
entries.answer: When more snow falls each year than melts, layers can build up. The weight presses the snow below into dense ice. When the mass becomes thick enough, gravity pulls it slowly downhill or outward. A moving mass of this kind is a glacier. It can bend and flow slowly even though it is solid. Rocks carried along the bottom may scrape and wear away the ground as the glacier moves.
facts: Glaciers may move while the air around them is below freezing.

entries.title: How can mud, sand, or shells become rock?
entries.answer: Sand, mud, and pieces of shells can settle when moving water or air slows down. A new layer may cover an older one. With enough layers, the weight above can squeeze grains together. Material left behind by water passing between them can act like glue. Over time, many loose grains become a solid sedimentary rock. Some kinds form directly from material dissolved in water rather than from separate pieces.
facts: Sandstone contains sand-sized grains.

entries.title: How can the ground stay frozen through summer?
entries.answer: Ground that stays at or below the freezing point of water for at least two years in a row is called permafrost. A layer above it can still thaw in warm weather and freeze again in winter. Some frozen ground contains a lot of ice. When that ice melts, the ground can settle and leave dips. Other permafrost contains very little ice. The word describes how long the ground stays that cold.
facts: Permafrost can occur in soil or rock. It does not have to be a solid piece of ice.

entries.title: How can there be water beneath the ground?
entries.answer: Some rain soaks through soil into openings between grains or into cracks in rock. If enough of those openings connect, water can move through them. A layer that stores water and lets enough pass through it to supply a well is called an aquifer. Water can come out again at a spring or enter a stream from below. Most underground water is in gaps rather than in one big open lake.
facts: The top of the saturated zone is often called the water table.

entries.title: How can things that lived in the sea become limestone?
entries.answer: Some limestone begins with bits of shells and other hard parts from life in water. The bits settle to the bottom and build layers. Material left between the pieces helps bind them into rock. Limestone can also form when dissolved minerals come out of water without shells. Much of it is rich in calcium carbonate. Water with a little natural acid can dissolve limestone slowly, giving some caves space to grow.
facts: Many fossils are found in limestone.

How can loose bits join to make a solid rock layer?
Why can hard parts remain when soft parts disappear?

entries.title: How does a hole become a natural rock arch?
entries.answer: In places such as Arches National Park, cracks split sandstone into long, narrow walls. Rain can get into cracks, and pieces of rock gradually break and fall away. Sometimes a weak part low on a wall disappears before the stone above it. If the stone overhead still joins both sides, it can stand as an arch. The rock keeps wearing away after an arch forms. An arch can collapse when it gets too weak.
facts: Many rock walls at Arches National Park are called fins.

entries.title: How does erosion leave a narrow tower of stone?
entries.answer: A hoodoo is a tall, narrow shape made by rock wearing away unevenly. At Bryce Canyon, water enters cracks and can freeze when it gets cold. Ice takes more room than liquid water and pushes cracks wider. Repeated freezing and thawing loosen pieces from a wall until parts can stand alone. A harder top layer can protect softer rock beneath it for a while. The tower’s sides are still being worn away.
facts: Rain can slowly dissolve part of the rock at Bryce Canyon.

entries.title: How does wind build a hill out of sand?
entries.answer: Wind can bounce small sand grains along the ground. If the wind slows near a plant, rock, or other obstacle, loose grains can pile up. On many dunes, sand climbs the gentler side facing the wind. It spills over the top and slides down the steeper side. Repeating this can move a dune little by little, even though each grain travels only a short way. Changes in wind can change the dune’s shape.
facts: Dunes can form inland as well as near beaches.

entries.title: How erosion carries rock and soil away
entries.answer: Erosion happens when water, wind, ice, or gravity moves soil and bits of rock. Rain can wash dirt from a path into a ditch. A river can carry sand across a whole valley. A glacier can drag bits of stone as it slides. Weathering is a different part of the story: it breaks rock down in place, as when water in a crack freezes and pushes the crack wider. Erosion moves those pieces somewhere else. Where the moving water slows down, sand and mud may settle and build up in a new place.
facts: Running water can carry sediment downhill.
Moving ice and wind can cause erosion too.

entries.title: How the three main kinds of rock form
entries.answer: Scientists group rocks by the way they formed. Igneous rock forms when melted rock cools and hardens. Sedimentary rock can form when layers of sand, mud, or other bits get pressed and stuck together over time. Metamorphic rock forms when heat or pressure changes rock that is already there, without melting it all. The same bit of material can go through more than one of these changes over a long time. For example, a rock can wear down into sand, and the sand can become part of a new rock.
facts: Sandstone is a kind of sedimentary rock.
Some igneous rocks form underground and others form at the surface.

entries.title: What are the rocky ridges left by glaciers?
entries.answer: A glacier can carry pebbles, boulders, and sand in or on the ice. When its edge melts, the rock may stay behind, making a ridge called a moraine. A ridge along the side shows part of a glacier’s former edge. A stripe of rock in the middle of a glacier can form where two streams of ice join and bring their rocky sides together. These ridges can last long after the ice is gone.
facts: A moraine can hold rocks of many sizes mixed together.

entries.title: What happens when melted rock cools?
entries.answer: Melted rock below the ground is called magma. If it reaches the surface, it is called lava. As either one cools and becomes solid, it forms igneous rock. Where magma cools slowly underground, grains of different minerals have more time to grow. A thin flow at the surface can cool quickly and have grains too small to see. Some kinds of melted rock become glass instead of forming many crystals.
facts: Granite is an igneous rock that forms underground.

entries.title: What minerals are
entries.answer: A mineral is a solid that forms in nature and has a certain kind of material and pattern inside it. Quartz is one mineral. The grains you see in a piece of granite can be different minerals, including quartz and feldspar. A single rock can hold several minerals mixed together. To tell minerals apart, people look at things like how hard they are. Some are soft enough to scratch with a fingernail. Others can leave a scratch on a piece of glass.
facts: Granite can contain quartz, feldspar, and mica.
Table salt can come from a mineral called halite.

entries.title: Which cave formations hang down and which grow up?
entries.answer: Water can pass through rock and carry dissolved material into a cave. As a drop hangs from the ceiling, it may leave a little solid mineral. The next drop can leave a little more. A formation hanging downward is a stalactite. Drops that hit the floor can add to a mound called a stalagmite. If both grow far enough, they can form a column from floor to ceiling.
facts: Some cave formations grow extremely slowly.

entries.title: Why are some volcanic islands lined up?
entries.answer: A hot spot can supply melted rock beneath a moving plate. A volcano may grow above the hot spot until it reaches the ocean surface and makes an island. The plate then carries the island farther along. A new volcano can form nearer the hot spot. Over a long time, this can leave a chain with younger volcanoes toward one end and older ones toward the other. The Hawaiian chain records this pattern.
facts: A hot spot can supply volcanoes far from a plate edge.

entries.title: Why can the ground suddenly sink into a hole?
entries.answer: Rainwater can slowly dissolve some kinds of rock underground, including limestone. The openings can grow as more water passes through. Sometimes soil slips into the opening a little at a time, leaving a shallow bowl on the surface. In other places a roof of soil holds up for a while and then drops, opening a deeper hole more quickly. Not every sinkhole happens in the same way.
facts: Sinkholes can form by gradual sinking or sudden collapse.

entries.title: Why can water flow straight out of a hillside?
entries.answer: A spring is a place where underground water reaches the surface. Rain or melted snow can sink through gaps in soil and rock. Water may collect above a layer that is slow to let it through. It moves along openings until those openings reach a stream bank, a hillside, or the bottom of a valley. That water can make a creek even when no rain is falling right above it.
facts: Some springs shrink or stop during a long dry period.

entries.title: Why can you see several colors in one piece of granite?
entries.answer: A polished piece of granite can show pink, white, gray, or dark grains that fit together. The grains are different minerals. They grew when melted rock cooled slowly underground. Slow cooling gave the minerals time to form pieces big enough to see. Granite may only become visible long after it cools, when the rock above it wears away. A cut countertop can reveal some of the same patterns as a boulder outdoors.
facts: Quartz and feldspar are common in granite.

entries.title: Why does a geyser erupt over and over?
entries.answer: A geyser has a narrow or twisted route below ground to water heated by nearby hot rocks. Water deeper down can become very hot under the weight of water above it. As some water turns to steam and pushes water out, the pressure deep down drops. More steam forms quickly and the geyser sprays hot water. After the burst, water can seep back into the openings so the process begins again.
facts: Most hot springs lack the kind of plumbing that lets a geyser erupt.

entries.title: Why does a river sometimes spread into nearby land?
entries.answer: Water reaches a river from streams, slopes, rain, and melting snow. If water comes in faster than it can flow away, the river rises. It may spill onto nearby flat land, called a floodplain. When water spreading there slows, some mud and sand can settle out. Over many floods, this can add material to the land near a river. During lower water, rivers may return to a smaller, deeper channel.
facts: Snowmelt and heavy rain can contribute to floods.

entries.title: Why does some volcanic rock look like glass?
entries.answer: Obsidian is a natural glass that can form when some kinds of lava cool quickly. The material becomes solid before crystals have time to grow very much. The surface can be shiny. A break often leaves a curved hollow that looks a bit like the inside of a shell. People in different parts of the world once used pieces of obsidian as cutting tools because a broken edge can be quite sharp.
facts: Many pieces of obsidian are dark, but the color can vary.

entries.title: Why is a glacial valley shaped like a U?
entries.answer: A river often cuts a narrow trench with sloping sides. A glacier can fill much more of that valley and rub against its bottom and sides. It can carve a broad floor and high walls. When the ice retreats, the valley may look like a U in a view from one end. A smaller glacier nearby can cut a shallower valley that ends high above the floor of the main valley.
facts: A fjord is a glacial valley flooded by seawater.
Some waterfalls pour out of side valleys.

entries.title: Why the ground shakes in an earthquake
entries.answer: An earthquake can start when rocks on each side of a break in Earth’s crust get stuck. The break is called a fault. Motion deep in Earth keeps pushing or pulling on the rocks. If they suddenly slip, the energy that built up spreads away as waves. When the waves reach the surface, the ground shakes. The shaking may be strong near the fault and weaker farther away. Scientists use instruments to record the waves and learn where the earthquake began.
facts: The shaking comes from waves moving through Earth.
Many earthquakes happen near the edges of tectonic plates.

entries.title: Why volcanoes erupt
entries.answer: A volcano has an opening where hot melted rock can reach Earth’s surface. The melted rock is called magma while it is below ground and lava once it comes out. Gas trapped in magma can help push it upward. Some eruptions send out streams of lava. Others blast out clouds of broken rock and tiny pieces called ash. As lava cools, it hardens into rock. After many eruptions, lava and ash can build a whole mountain or add new land to an island.
facts: Volcanic ash is made of tiny pieces of hard material.
A volcano can make new land when lava cools and hardens.
